image_description:
1. **Chart type**: Sankey diagram / flow diagram.

2. **Layout techniques**:  
- Uses **flows/links** connecting categories across stages.  
- **Width of bands/nodes** encodes magnitude.  
- No faceting or small multiples.  
- Uses **color** to distinguish different flow groups/outcome paths.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Process stage / category (e.g., attempted crossings, encounters, processed under Title 8, expelled under Title 42, deportation order, etc.) | Categorical/nominal | Node position, text labels |
| Number of people / cases (e.g., 3.1 million, 2.5 million, 565k, etc.) | Quantitative | Width of nodes and flow bands; numeric labels |
| Flow connection between categories | Categorical/nominal (relational) | Connecting bands/links between nodes |
| Outcome/path grouping | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue of nodes and flow bands |
| Time period: 2023 / fiscal year 2023 | Temporal | Title/subtitle text annotation |

comments.raw_comment:
I notice that 3.1 million people attempted cross the U.S.'s southern border in 2023. I notice that 600,000 immigrants entered undetected. I also noticed that 870,000 immigrants were deported, left voluntarily, or expelled from the U.S. Finally I notice that 1.8 million immigrants are still in legal limbo or in ongoing proceedings. This means that the majority of immigrants that attempted to enter the U.S. through our southern border in 2023 succeeded. I wonder why some immigrants are expelled under Title 42 and why some are processed under Title 8. I wonder how so many immigrants are able to enter the U.S. undetected. Clearly our border control cannot account for the millions of migrants attempting to immigrate to the U.S. I also what caused 180,000 migrants to leave voluntarily as this journey through or southern border is apparently very treacherous. I wonder if we will make progress in improving our border control and granting people citizenship in a more efficient way. This relates to myself and my community as the migrant crisis is a topic of conversation at my family dinner table as well as on the news frequently. This has been one of the topics in politics that I have been hearing about constantly for the past few years.

Migrant Mania

comments.raw_comment: I initially noticed that almost all who attempted to cross were encountered by U.S Customs and Border Protection, with six hundred thousand entering undetected. This suggests the United States' high-security borders. About 2 million encountered were processed under Title 8, and only two thousand have gotten relief and are not in ongoing procedures. This may mean that the process is complex and lengthy. Of the 2.5 million encountered, a substantial number were expelled under Title 42. I wonder how 600-thousand were able to enter undetected, being that the border seemingly has a lot of control. Additionally, I wonder what the graph would look like if we could see the outcomes of those who entered undetectedly. I wonder how this graph looked in the past, and how it will look in upcoming years. This relates to me and my community, as it is important to recognize our country's border policies, given it is a controversial topic in the news very frequently. "Southern Border Struggles and Successes"

comments.raw_comment:
This graph shows the attempted crossings at the U.S. southern border in 2023. In this graph, 1.8 million people who attempted to cross the border are in ongoing proceedings or legal limbo while 870,000 people have deportation orders, expulsion, etc. In addition, 600,000 immigrants entered undetected. Clearly, from this statistic, the border is not as secure as the government makes it seem as there is still a significant amount of people sneaking into this country illegally.  Title 42 says that when non-citizens enter the US on an illegal basis they will be processed for removal. Title 42 does not impose immigration or criminal consequences on migrants. Therefore, migrants who are expelled can repeatedly try and cross the border. I wonder how many migrants this past year attempted to cross the border for the 2nd, 3rd, or 4th time as a result of this law. I wonder how many of those migrants found undetected ways to enter. I also wonder why people would travel thousands of miles to this country and voluntarily depart once they begin being processed under Title 8. Is being processed really that bad? 180,000 people voluntarily departed once they began being processed under Title 8! This relates to me because my mom is an immigration lawyer and her job is to help people achieve immigration status in the United States. I am sure she is very familiar with all of this. 
"How Immigrants Make Their Way into the US"

Most of the attempted US border crosses occur through border processes, such as under title 8, or through an exception such as under title 42, like during a pandemic or public health concern. Under title 8, most of the crossings occurred according to new immigration court cases. Also, an estimated fifth of the attempted US border crossings are undetected.

I wonder what the “relief granted” portion of title 8 crossings means. It is such a small fraction of the total US crossings, at only 2.7k, so I wonder how or why these occur.

This information could be important to educating not only immigrants, but citizens of the occurrences at the southern US border. Families whose success have depended upon entry to America can learn and know about such information, as well as people whose families have resided in the US for generations. It’s also interesting to me, as my dad is an immigrant who crossed the southern border.

Out of 2.5 million encounters in this graph, 1.8 million immigrants are either still pending legal proceedings or are in legal limbo. Out of them, only 2,700 have been granted relief or residency, while 870,000 have been deported. 3.1 million people tried to cross the southern border into the United States in 2023; 1.8 million of them succeeded in doing so, 870,000 of them left the country, and about 602,700 were either ignored or granted amnesty.

In an effort to provide for their families and become financially successful in the future, many immigrants, both first and second-generation, put a lot of effort into their employment. comments.raw_comment:
This graph shows how many people were believed to have attempted to cross the United States' southern border in 2023. In total, it is estimated that 3.1 million people tried to enter the US through the southern border. Out of the total, 1.8 million are going through legal endeavors because of their status, 870,000 were pushed back to their native country, and around 602,700 people have gone undetected or were granted amnesty. Considering so many people were turned away from the US under Title 42, what will happen now that Title 42 has come to an end? Title 42 was lenient in the sense that, unlike Title 8, people attempting to cross the southern border could try again and again; no one was banned. Will future policies on immigration begin to get more strict? Will those already integrated into American society who may lack citizenship be harmed? As New Jersey is an asylum state, many immigrants in my community have not been granted citizenship yet. In the upcoming presidential election, with immigration and borders being a highlighted topic, I worry for the members of my community and how this could impact them.

“Crossing The Southern Border: The Odds of Success”

comments.raw_comment: In this graph, it is displaying the different things that happened to migrants who attempted to cross the southern border in 2023. I noticed that there were 3.1 million attempts to cross the border, but only 600k entered undetected. I also noticed that the majority (1.8 million) of migrants were in ongoing proceedings or legal limbo compared to 870k facing deportation order, expulsion, etc. Additionally, I noticed that out of the people who faced deportation, order, expulsion, etc, the most (565k) were expelled under Title 42. I wonder what Title 42 and Title 8 are and why there are more people processed under Title 8 than expelled under Title 42. I also wonder why such little relief (2.7k) is granted to people. This relates to my community because I know many people who immigrated to the United States and I wonder if they had to face any of the processes that are listed in the graph. Also, I always hear about immigration issues in politics and know that it is presently a very highly debated topic. My headline for this graph would be: “Crossing the Border - A Not So Easy Process”.

I notice that the majority of people who attempted crossing at the US southern border are in ongoing proceedings or legal limbo (1.8 million). I also notice that many of the people processed under Title 8 do not have an expedited removal or voluntary departure (365k). The most direction expulsion is through Title 42 (565k).

I wonder why so many individuals are in ongoing proceedings. Are they in jail during this time? I also wonder if other immigrants have similar rates of deportation. It would likely be more difficult to enter the US undetected if immigrating from overseas, but I am curious whether these individuals arrive in comparably extenuating circumstances.

This impacts my community because immigration affects the country's economy and atmosphere. Although I do not live in the South, policy on immigration still plays a role in elections. Furthermore, immigrants bring ideas and traditions from their home countries that contribute to our "melting pot."

comments.raw_comment:
What do you notice? The graph shows what happens to migrants who attempt to cross the southern border of the United States of America. A good chunk of migrants are able to pass into America undocumented, while the majority encounter US forces. Of these approximated 2.5 million people who are processed by the US, another chunk is expelled or undergo other forms of deportations. However, the majority are put into the legal system and are in limbo, awaiting a court answer.
I wonder why so many people are in long-term legal limbo. Immigration from the southern border is such a big issue, so why hasn't the government allocated more resources to processing immigration cases? If the judicial process was easier, less people would feel the need to enter America undocumented. 
As someone who lives in America, I think that it's truly wrong that so many people who want to live here are hindered at every step by the government of the very place they want to live in. 
Headline: WHERE DO THEY GO? MIGRANTS IN AMERICA

In this graph, I noticed the amount of migrants who attempted to cross the U.S. southern border in 2023 is a lot, approximately 3.1 million!! I notice that among these illegal migrants about 600,000 entered the US without detection. The process of becoming a US citizen is a tough one, which is why many desperate migrants feel the need to cross the southern border into the US illegally. The majority of immigrants who are not forced or choose to leave the United States are still in a place of uncertainty and a state of processing, about 1.8 million are still being processed. Immigration and the safety of the Southern border is a major topic in this present political climate. I wonder when the government is going to get its act together and fix its border protection laws. Recently, an illegal Venezuelan immigrant murdered a University of Georgia student and has a lengthy criminal record. This shows that the immigration process and the process of border protection need to be changed to prevent more killings of Americans. This affects me and my community because I am an American citizen, and I must be educated on this topic that is quite prevalent in politics today.

1) In this graph, 1.8 million immigrants remain in legal limbo or have continuing processes, out of 2.5 million interactions. Of these, 870,000 have been deported, with only 2,700 granted relief or residency. In 2023, 3.1 million persons attempted to enter the United States over the southern border, 1.8 million completed legal procedures, 870,000 returned to their home countries, and approximately 602,700 went unnoticed or awarded amnesty.

2) The end of Title 42 raises questions about the future of undocumented immigrants and the duration of their legal limbo, as it was lenient in allowing repeated attempts to cross the southern border, unlike Title 8. The estimated number of undocumented immigrants and their duration in legal limbo remains uncertain.

3) My community of Perth Amboy, an attraction for immigrants, is concerned about the persistent immigration challenges that its inhabitants encounter. Many first and second-generation immigrants work hard to improve the lives of their families in the hopes of achieving financial success in the future. The troubling data show that only 2,700 people received assistance, while over 800,000 were deported, demonstrating the community's continued hardships.

comments.raw_comment:
I noticed that making through the border undetected is very rare in attempted crossings on the Southern border. Most migrants encounter border patrol and after that usually enter legal proceedings and legal battles to stay in the country. Meanwhile others are usually deported while only a small fraction get to actually stay in the country.

I wonder what Title 42 is and how it managed to deport almost 600k migrants in 2023 alone.  I also wonder how long the legal processes take when migrants are caught by border patrol.

This relates to me and my community as the border crisis is at an all time high as migrants attempt to escape their past in search for a better future. Also as migrants make it through the border they are settling in societies such as mine in Perth Amboy NJ.

Operation Southern Border: Migrants vs Legal System

comments.raw_comment:
This graph shows how many people were believed to have attempted to cross the United States' southern border in 2023. In total, it is estimated that 3.1 million people tried to enter the US through the southern border. Out of the total, 1.8 million are going through legal endeavors because of their status, 870,000 were pushed back to their native country, and around 602,700 people have gone undetected or were granted amnesty. Considering so many people were turned away from the US under Title 42, what will happen now that Title 42 has come to an end? Title 42 was lenient in the sense that, unlike Title 8, people attempting to cross the southern border could try again and again; no one was banned. Will future policies on immigration begin to get more strict? Will those already integrated into American society who may lack citizenship be harmed? As New Jersey is an asylum state, many immigrants in my community have not been granted citizenship yet. In the upcoming presidential election, with immigration and borders being a highlighted topic, I worry for the members of my community and how this could impact them.

“Crossing The Southern Border: The Odds of Success”

This also relates to my community because NJ is one of the states with the highest population of immigrants. 

4) The Border Experience

comments.raw_comment:
This graph shows how many people were believed to have attempted to cross the United States' southern border in 2023. In total, it is estimated that 3.1 million people tried to enter the US through the southern border. Out of the total, 1.8 million are going through legal endeavors because of their status, 870,000 were pushed back to their native country, and around 602,700 people have gone undetected or were granted amnesty. Considering so many people were turned away from the US under Title 42, what will happen now that Title 42 has come to an end? Title 42 was lenient in the sense that, unlike Title 8, people attempting to cross the southern border could try again and again; no one was banned. Will future policies on immigration begin to get more strict? Will those already integrated into American society who may lack citizenship be harmed? As New Jersey is an asylum state, many immigrants in my community have not been granted citizenship yet. In the upcoming presidential election, with immigration and borders being a highlighted topic, I worry for the members of my community and how this could impact them.

“Crossing The Southern Border: The Odds of Success”

Yet we have the education to realize that wrong is happening at the border and in court for migrants at the Southern border, and we wish for change. I've always been frustrated by the way the Southern border has been handled and how those wishing to stay in the US are callously left in limbo by paperwork and trivialities. This graph shows just more of the same, which it should not. There needs to be changed, and I hope our generation can rise and make that change.

4.

comments.raw_comment:
I noticed that the majority of people who cross the border into the United States and are detected by border patrol are either deported or have to deal with legal issues. A very small number of people are granted relief, about 2.7K according to the graph, compared to the 1.8 million people who are in ongoing legal proceedings or the 870K people who are deported. There is a larger amount of people who enter the United States through the southern border and stay, both detected and undetected, than the amount of people who enter the United States through the southern border and are expelled.
I wonder why out of all of the people who have been in immigration court cases, only a few of them have been granted relief. Only 2.7K people have been granted relief, while more than 600 times that are still dealing with legal proceedings.
This does not have a large impact on my community since I live in a small town in New Hampshire. New Hampshire is very far away from the southern border, so the majority of the issues that are happening in those states don’t affect us. Since I live in a small town, it is very unlikely that the people who cross the border will be moved here. The most it could affect me is hearing about the migrants being moved to the larger cities in New Hampshire, such as Nashua, Manchester, and Concord. I would hear people would talk about the news stories, but that would be the largest extent of effect to me.
What’s Actually Going On With the Migrants At the Border.

1. I noticed that about 80% of migrants are encountered by border control and legal action, whereas they estimate around 20% of migrants enter without being noticed. Also, about 80% of the migrants caught are then pushed into the court system under Title 8 which outlines how migrants should be handled at the border. The graph shows different paths that break off from each other and then lead to new outcomes, but all 2.5 million migrants found will ultimately be faced with a negative journey in the legal or deportation path. 
2. I wonder if this graph will push for any legislation to fix this overwhelming issue. I also wonder how this graph breaks down the section regarding processing under Title 8. What actions or decisions are given to migrants before extreme measures are taken? 
3. The problem of migrants coming over the border impacts my community in many ways. It causes an overwhelming amount of people to take over cities and communities. As these people are technically (though they should not be) illegal, they cannot find places to live, eat, or be employed. This can add to the homeless population of communities ultimately affecting how that community functions. However, I do not want to look at this problem as entirely negative because I do think migrants can add a lot to a community. They bring diversity through ideas, food, creativity, and more. 
4. “The impenetrable journey to crossing the U.S. southern border in 2023.”

comments.raw_comment:
1. 3.1 million people attempted border crossings into U.S. territory. 600 thousand went undetected, 565 thousand were expelled under Title 42 (and later deported), and 2.5 million were processed under Title 8. Out of those 2.5 million, 185 thousand faced expedited removal and were later deported, 180 thousand voluntarily departed and were later deported, 1.5 million were added to court cases, and 300 thousand were paroled. As a remainder of the 2.5 million, 1.8 million are in ongoing proceedings or “legal limbo”.
	What I took away from this was that the majority of people immigrating into the U.S. are currently involved in court cases/legal limbo. Only 2.7 thousand people were let into the U.S, which was really surprising and sad to see, considering 3.1 million people tried to get into the U.S. which means roughly only 0.08% of people got into the U.S. legally.
2. How do they know that 600 thousand people made it undetected?
How do they know that this estimate is accurate?
3. For me, this doesn’t really have an impact on my community, since we aren’t that close to the Southern immigration flow. Because of this, I can't really speak from experience, but I will say that the way the borders have been handled lately, is just not good enough.

comments.raw_comment:
I notice that little less than 60% of those who attempt border crossings make it to a position where they could be accepted into the US. I also notice that the estimated number of undetected crossings into the US is eerily similar to the number of those expelled under Title 42 by US Customs or Border Protections. Only 2700 people out of the 1.5 million new-for-2023 immigration court cases receive relief and are allowed to stay in the US.

I wonder why so few people (2.7k) eventually receive relief when the vast majority (1.8m) of people who are hoping to stay in the US are stuck in legal limbo or trying their best to make a case in an ongoing proceeding

In the tri-state area, we don’t necessarily take the brunt of the Southern border immigration flow. Yet we have the education to realize that wrong is happening at the border and in court for migrants at the Southern border, and we wish for change. I've always been frustrated by the way the Southern border has been handled and how those wishing to stay in the US are callously left in limbo by paperwork and trivialities. This graph shows just more of the same, which it should not. There needs to be change, and I hope our generation can rise and make that change.

The Quantified Flow of Southern Border Crossings.

comments.raw_comment:
1. What do you notice?
The majority of migrants do not end up in a state of resolutions, but are caught up in “legal limbo” or ongoing cases. The next largest group is deported or expelled, while only a tiny fraction of the people (less than 0.1%) are granted relief legally. The only realistic way for them to enter the country is to do so undetected, which an estimated 600k do, since an encounter with customs all but guarantees rejection or an indeterminate result.

2. What do you wonder?

What does deportation/expulsion look like? Is there a specific protocol for bringing them back, or do they just get told to walk in the other direction? Also, what differentiates those granted relief from the vast majority who are not? Is there a special criteria they must meet? Lastly, what are “non-border cases”, and how do they enter the picture?

3. What impact does this have on you and your community?
I’m not sure that there are many migrants who arrive in my local area, but this certainly has an impact on my larger, national community. The large number of migrants can have an impact on cities that they arrive in. In some cases, this means filling jobs which are unwanted by other parts of the population, or in some cases by putting a stress on welfare systems. It also has an impact on politics, since immigration issues can polarize people’s views.

comments.raw_comment:
1. My eyes were first drawn to the complexity of the graphic which could be indicative of the complexity of seeking asylum and safety in the United States. As my eyes wandered around the graphic I noticed that the vast majority of migrants get deported whether immediately or eventually but most usually get deported after long and expensive legal battles with our country’s judicial system. I finally made it to the bottom of the graphic and saw that out of 3.1 million asylum seekers who enter our country each year, only 2.7 thousand are granted asylum and relief but only after a long journey from the desert to the courts that can take up to a decade to wrap up. 

2. It makes me wonder how much time, resources, and money would be saved if we provided migrants with an easy and accessible path to citizenship.

3. The influx of undocumented people into our cities causes issues with sustainable houses, clothing, and food, especially in the winter. Unfortunately, undocumented people are not granted the same courtesy that US citizens and permanent residents are granted in terms of rights, jobs, and resources. As a US permanent resident, I understand the complexities and intricacies of gaining US citizenship and navigating through immigration courts and I will always advocate for the recognition and naturalization of undocumented people in the US.

4. A Journey to Futility: Crossing the US Southern Border

comments.raw_comment:
1. What do you notice?
I notice many things about this graph. One striking statistic is that only 2,700 immigrants, out of the 3.1 million person total, become legal citizens of the United States (0.08%). Additionally, 185k immigrants are forced into expedited removal which the National Immigration Forum describes as deportation in as little as one day without a hearing. Interestingly, about 58% of cases result in proceedings or “legal limbo”. 
2. What do you wonder?
I wonder how are expedited removals and deportations carried out. Are the immigrants literally put on planes or vans back into their home countries? How is the total of undocumented immigrants calculated? Why do some choose voluntary departure? Lastly, how does the US court system determine who is eligible or who should deserve relief? How can we help process immigration cases faster and help immigrants access better opportunities?
3. What impact does this have on you and your community?
The government needs some way to pay for all of the resources needed to deal with this issue. This money comes from US taxes. This can affect many communities with an influx of immigrants, documented or not. This topic of a great increase in immigration does not majorly impact where I am from as I do not live close to the border or any major cities. 
4. Write a catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea.
The Southern Border Byproduct: What is Really Happening With Illegal Immigration?

comments.raw_comment:
1.
I noticed ⅕ that the migrants entered the US without being detected. Out of the 3.1 million who have entered the US through the southern border, 2.5 million encountered U.S. customs and border protection. The result of this was that 1.5 million more court cases were added this year after being processed under Title 8. 
2.
I wonder why there are no new laws enforced or made to stop or reduce the amount of migrants entering undetected. I wonder if this number will continue to grow and how much more will need to enter in order for there to be change. Titles 8 and 42 were presented on the data. I also wonder what determines a person to be under either 8 or 42. 
3.
These migrants who are entering the U.S. need a place to go. Whether it's planned for where they are going or unplanned, they are traveling throughout the U.S., most with the idea of getting away from the Southern borders as much as possible, thus moving north. This can impact our community greatly if we start to receive migrants at an increasing rate. Jobs will be harder to get, prices could increase, and more living space and conditions will be at stake. Currently, we don’t see a lot of this in New England because it's such an expensive place to live. 
4.
2023 in Review of Migrants Crossing the Southern Boarder.

comments.raw_comment:
I notice that the combination of the approximate amount of immigrants who entered undetected or were given relief (602,700) was less than the total immigrants who were denied access or voluntarily departed (930k). Out of the whole, about  1,567,300 immigrants are in legal limbo, which is about 50.6% of the whole. 

I wonder why there is no new legislation passed to regulate the border cases. I know that there is intense political gridlock on this very polarizing issue, however the more time migrants spend at the border, the more money the government is spending anyways. If the government were to create better legal infrastructure, and yes, spend more money now to create it, the process might be expedited and cause less distress for the government and the migrants. 

I am a child of two immigrants who emigrated to the US legally. However, it has become increasingly difficult to emigrate to the US because of the practices at the border and seemingly never-ending paperwork, put in place to make the process drawn out. I do believe that there needs to be a better vetting system of candidates, in both that dangerous people are not let into the US, but also that people who deserve legal entry are granted this. There has long been abuse of migrant labor through H1 and green cards, but the malpractice at the border and abuse of migrants saddens me, especially when a key pillar of American government is equality of opportunity.  

Give US your tired & poor; but only if you're a citizen
